edges.mechanism: The Fed's balance sheet is the numerator of net liquidity: what it buys, it pays for with money that did not exist before.
Cash parked overnight at the Fed is cash not in the market. Reverse repo draining is liquidity being released without the Fed buying anything.
Money in the Treasury's account has left the banking system. A tax date or a heavy auction fills it; government spending empties it back out.

edges.breaks: Fails completely when the reason liquidity is rising is that something broke — 2008 and March 2020 both saw liquidity surge into falling equities.
edges.mechanism: More money loose in the system has to go somewhere, and the deepest market is where it goes first.

edges.breaks: Crypto-native shocks — an exchange failure, a forced liquidation cascade — swamp the liquidity signal for weeks at a time.
edges.mechanism: Bitcoin has no earnings to fall back on, so its price is close to a pure function of how much spare money exists.
A growing BoJ balance sheet is more yen in existence, and more yen borrowed cheaply to buy assets elsewhere.
The two-year is mostly an average of what the Fed is expected to do, so it follows the policy rate closely and leads it at turns.
edges.why: the source sits still between decisions, so its day-to-day changes are almost all zero and a correlation on them means nothing

edges.mechanism: A three-month bill is very nearly a bet on the overnight rate over three months.
edges.why: the source sits still between decisions, so its day-to-day changes are almost all zero and a correlation on them means nothing

edges.mechanism: The ten-year contains the expected path of short rates, so the front end pulls it — but only partly, since the rest is term premium.

edges.breaks: Decouples precisely when supply or inflation risk is the driver — the 30-year rises alone, which is the bond market pricing government borrowing rather than Fed policy.
edges.mechanism: The long end moves together most days; when it does not, the difference is the story.
The curve is the ten-year minus the two-year, so the front end rising flattens it by construction.
The other half of the same arithmetic: the long end rising steepens it.

edges.breaks: This is the edge with no series on this board — the supply side is not measurable here. What you can see is whether the 30-year rose anyway after an announcement that was supposed to help, which is the whole reason it is drawn.
edges.mechanism: More bonds sold than buyers want at today's price clears at a lower price, which is the same thing as a higher yield. The Treasury can change how much it sells and buy old bonds back, but it cannot make anyone want them.
edges.why: no series published for Treasury issuance & buybacks

edges.mechanism: A nominal yield is a real yield plus expected inflation. If the market expects more inflation and demands the same real return, the nominal yield has to rise.
The other half of the same identity — and the half that matters for whether a rise is a growth story or an inflation story.

edges.breaks: Slow and structural. On any given week it is invisible; over a year of JGB normalisation it is one of the biggest forces on the long end.
edges.mechanism: Japanese institutions are among the largest owners of foreign bonds on earth. When they can earn a real yield at home they need Treasuries less, and the marginal buyer steps back.

edges.breaks: Overwhelmed whenever the Fed is moving faster than the BoJ — the gap between the two, not either level, is what the currency trades on.
edges.mechanism: Higher yields at home make the yen worth holding, so it strengthens and the dollar buys fewer of them.

edges.breaks: Reverses when yields are rising because growth is strong — early in a recovery both go up together, and reading that as a warning is the classic mistake.
edges.mechanism: A higher discount rate makes every future dollar of profit worth less today. Nothing about the businesses changed; the arithmetic under them did.

edges.breaks: Same exception, amplified: in an earnings upgrade cycle the growth beats the discount rate and both rise together.
edges.mechanism: Technology profits sit further in the future than the market's, so discounting them harder costs more. This is the same edge as the S&P one, with a longer lever.

edges.breaks: Fails when the yield is rising because the US is the problem — a fiscal scare pushes yields up and the dollar down at the same time, which is the tell that it is a credibility story rather than a rate story.
edges.mechanism: Money chases yield across borders. A higher US yield relative to everywhere else pulls capital into dollars to earn it.
A 30-year mortgage is priced off the 10-year Treasury plus a spread for prepayment and credit risk. This is the closest thing to arithmetic on the board.
A company borrows at the government's rate plus its own spread, so the government's rate passes straight through.

edges.breaks: Has broken for long stretches since 2022, and central-bank buying is the usual explanation: a buyer accumulating reserves for political reasons is not comparing yields at all.
edges.mechanism: Gold pays no interest. The higher the real yield on a government bond, the more you give up by holding metal instead — that opportunity cost is gold's entire valuation model.
The other half of gold's case: it is bought as insurance against money losing value, and breakevens are the market's estimate of exactly that.
The same opportunity-cost argument as gold, applied to another asset with no yield — but far noisier, because bitcoin's own cycle usually dominates.

edges.breaks: Regime-dependent and frequently absent. Bitcoin has rallied through rising-yield stretches more than once, and when it does the liquidity and adoption stories are simply larger than the discount-rate one.
edges.mechanism: Bitcoin has no cash flow to discount, so it competes head-on with the risk-free rate: the more a government bond pays for doing nothing, the higher the bar for holding something that pays nothing at all.

edges.breaks: Vanishes whenever bitcoin is trading on something of its own — an ETF flow, a halving, a failure.
edges.mechanism: Bitcoin is priced in dollars and bought largely with borrowed ones. A stronger dollar is both a lower quoted number and a tighter world.
A disorderly long end unsettles equities, because it means the discount rate itself has stopped being predictable.
When the price of government bonds becomes unpredictable, every risk model that uses them widens its estimates, and lenders demand more to hold credit.

edges.breaks: Both can widen and rally together in the first weeks of a recovery, when default risk falls faster than equity enthusiasm returns.
edges.mechanism: Credit investors are paid to worry and they usually move first. A widening spread is the cheapest early warning on this board.
Small companies borrow at floating rates and refinance often, so credit conditions reach them first and hardest.
An investment-grade company's borrowing cost is the government yield plus this spread, by definition.

edges.breaks: Not a cause. This edge is drawn because people read it as one — the VIX is a restatement of what equities just did, not a warning about what they will do.
edges.mechanism: Mechanically inverse most days, because the VIX is priced off the same options that get bid when equities fall.
Bitcoin is the last thing bought with borrowed money and the first thing sold when that money is called back.
Emerging markets borrow in dollars and earn in local currency. A stronger dollar makes their debt heavier without anyone borrowing another cent — the world's margin call.

edges.breaks: Both rise together in a genuine flight to safety, when the demand for anything safe overwhelms the quotation effect.
edges.mechanism: Gold is quoted in dollars, so a stronger dollar mechanically lowers the number even before any change in demand.
Priced in dollars and bought by everyone else, so a stronger dollar makes it dearer for the buyers who actually use it.

edges.breaks: Almost always. Oil's supply shocks are larger than the currency effect; treat this edge as a background force rather than a driver.
edges.mechanism: The same quotation effect, usually swamped by whatever OPEC or a war is doing.

edges.breaks: Thailand's trade surplus and gold-linked flows through Thai dealers have repeatedly held the baht up when the model said it should fall.
edges.mechanism: The baht is not in the dollar index but trades with the region against it, so broad dollar strength usually shows up here too.
A falling baht makes Thai assets cheaper to foreigners but signals money leaving, and the leaving usually dominates.
A weaker yuan makes Chinese exports cheaper and squeezes the countries competing with them for the same orders.
Japanese exporters earn abroad and report at home, so a weaker yen inflates their profits in yen terms without a single extra unit sold.

edges.breaks: Only binds during an actual unwind. In calm markets the correlation is close to noise, which is why the yen is a tripwire here rather than a signal.
edges.mechanism: The carry trade: borrow yen at nearly nothing, buy something that yields more. A strengthening yen forces that borrowed money home, and the highest-beta positions are sold first.
Energy is an input to everything physical, so the market revises its inflation expectations almost immediately when crude moves.
The same barrel, priced at two different loading points. The gap between them is US export capacity, not two different markets.
Thailand imports nearly all of its energy. Expensive oil is a direct transfer out of Thai household spending and corporate margins.

edges.breaks: Positive whenever oil is rising because global demand is strong; the sign here is about supply shocks specifically.
edges.mechanism: Expensive energy is a tax on the consumer and on margins — but it also lifts the energy sector, so the index effect is smaller than the household one.
Silver follows gold's monetary story with more leverage, and adds an industrial one on top.
China is roughly half of world copper demand. Its construction and grid spending is the marginal buyer.
Most of the developing world sells commodities. A rising copper price is their terms of trade improving.
Chinese demand and Chinese tourists are Thailand's largest single external input.
The same companies and the same policy, priced by two different sets of investors.
Semiconductors are the largest and most volatile block inside the index, and the AI trade runs through them.
Memory is Korea's largest export. The chip cycle and the KOSPI are close to the same instrument.
Taiwan's index is substantially one company, and that company is the semiconductor cycle.
Global risk appetite is set in New York and exported everywhere else.
Thailand moves on foreign flows, and foreign flows move on how the world feels about risk — which is why Thai stocks fall on days when nothing happened in Thailand.
Ether carries bitcoin's move plus the risk appetite inside crypto itself.
Housing finance reaches the domestic economy — builders, suppliers, regional banks — before it reaches anything global.

nodes.label: Fed funds rate
nodes.up: Money costs more overnight — the Fed is leaning against the economy
nodes.what: What banks actually pay to borrow from each other overnight, which is the one interest rate the Federal Reserve sets directly. Every other rate in the world is priced off this one plus an argument.

nodes.label: Fed balance sheet
nodes.up: The Fed is holding more assets — QE, or emergency lending
nodes.what: Everything the Federal Reserve owns. It grows when the Fed buys bonds with money it creates (QE) and shrinks when it lets them mature (QT). This is the number people mean when they say 'money printing'.

nodes.label: Reverse repo
nodes.up: More cash is sitting idle at the Fed instead of in the market
nodes.what: Cash that money-market funds park at the Fed overnight because they cannot find anywhere better. It is liquidity that exists but is not being used — money in the waiting room.

nodes.label: Treasury cash account
nodes.up: The Treasury is holding more cash — money drained out of the market
nodes.what: The US government's own chequing account at the Fed. When it fills up (after a tax date or a big bond auction) that money has left the banking system; when it is spent down, the money comes back.

nodes.label: Net liquidity
nodes.up: There is more money loose in the system looking for somewhere to go
nodes.what: The Fed's balance sheet minus the two places money hides: reverse repo and the Treasury's cash account. It is the closest single number to 'how much money is actually circulating', and it is the tide that lifts and drops risk assets without anybody announcing anything.

nodes.label: Bank of Japan assets
nodes.up: The BoJ is still the buyer of last resort — cheap yen keeps flowing out
nodes.what: Everything the Bank of Japan owns. Japan ran the world's largest and longest money-printing programme, and the cheap yen it created funded asset purchases everywhere else. When it shrinks, that funding leaves.

nodes.label: Treasury issuance & buybacks
nodes.up: The government is selling more debt than buyers want at today's price
nodes.what: How much new government debt is being sold, and whether the Treasury is buying old bonds back. This board cannot measure it — there is no daily series for it — so it sits here as a named cause with no number, and the only honest way to read it is through what the 30-year does next.

nodes.label: US 2-year yield
nodes.up: The market expects the Fed to keep rates higher for longer
nodes.what: What the government pays to borrow for two years. It is mostly a bet on what the Fed will do over that window, so it moves on policy expectations rather than on anything structural.

nodes.label: US 10-year yield
nodes.up: Borrowing for a decade got more expensive — every valuation on earth resets
nodes.what: The world's discount rate. Roughly the average overnight rate expected over ten years plus a premium for the risk of holding it that long. Every valuation model starts here: when it rises, cash flows far in the future are worth less today, and the companies whose profits are furthest away fall the most.

nodes.label: US 30-year yield
nodes.up: The long end is demanding more — usually about supply or inflation, not the Fed
nodes.what: The long end of the curve. The Fed has the least control here, so this is where worries about government borrowing and long-run inflation show up first. When people say 'the bond market is voting', they mean this.

nodes.label: Yield curve (10y − 2y)
nodes.up: The curve is steepening — long money is getting dearer relative to short
nodes.what: The gap between ten-year and two-year borrowing costs. Negative means the market expects rates to fall, which historically means it expects a recession. Steepening from below zero is the classic late signal.

nodes.label: 10-year real yield
nodes.up: You are paid more to hold bonds after inflation — the bar every other asset must clear
nodes.what: The ten-year yield with expected inflation stripped out — what a bond actually earns you in purchasing power. This, not the headline yield, is what gold competes against, because gold pays nothing at all.

nodes.label: 10-year breakeven
nodes.up: The market is pricing more inflation over the next decade
nodes.what: How much inflation the bond market expects each year for ten years, read off the gap between ordinary and inflation-linked bonds. It is the market's forecast, not the government's statistic, and it moves daily.

nodes.label: Japan 10-year yield
nodes.up: Japanese money can finally earn something at home instead of abroad
nodes.what: What Japan pays to borrow for ten years. It was pinned near zero for a generation, which pushed Japanese institutions — among the world's largest bond buyers — into foreign debt. Every basis point it rises is a reason for that money to come home.

nodes.label: High-yield spread
nodes.up: Lenders want more to lend to weak companies — the free warning signal
nodes.what: The extra yield demanded to lend to companies with poor credit, over lending to the government. Credit investors are paid to be pessimistic and they are usually early: this widens before equities fall, not after.

nodes.label: Investment-grade spread
nodes.up: Even the good borrowers are being charged more — stress reaching the core
nodes.what: The same measure for companies nobody worries about. When this widens as well, the problem has stopped being about weak borrowers and started being about the price of credit itself.

nodes.label: MOVE index
nodes.up: The bond market has stopped agreeing with itself about where rates go
nodes.what: Volatility in the bond market — the VIX of Treasuries. It matters more than equity volatility, because every bank and fund on earth sizes its positions off the price of government bonds. When this jumps, positions everywhere get smaller whether anyone wanted that or not.

nodes.label: VIX
nodes.up: Options on US equities cost more — somebody is paying up for protection
nodes.what: What it costs to insure the S&P 500 for the next month. Famous, and less useful than its fame suggests: it mostly tells you what already happened today, whereas credit spreads tend to tell you first.

nodes.label: Dollar index
nodes.up: The dollar is stronger — the world's margin call gets more expensive
nodes.what: The dollar against a basket of rich-world currencies. Most of the world's debt is written in dollars, so a rising dollar makes everyone else's debt heavier without anybody borrowing another cent. It is the single most reliable tightening signal there is.

nodes.label: USD / JPY
nodes.up: The yen is weaker — the cheapest funding currency on earth stays cheap
nodes.what: How many yen a dollar buys. It is the carry trade's thermometer: borrow yen at nearly nothing, buy anything that yields more. When the yen strengthens sharply that trade unwinds, and everything bought with borrowed yen gets sold at once.

nodes.label: USD / CNY
nodes.up: The yuan is weaker — Beijing is tolerating, or exporting, deflation
nodes.what: How many yuan a dollar buys, which is managed rather than free. A weaker yuan makes Chinese goods cheaper everywhere, which exports China's deflation to everyone else — and squeezes competitors like Korea, Taiwan and Thailand.

nodes.label: USD / THB
nodes.up: The baht is weaker — your dollar holdings are worth more in the money you spend
nodes.what: How many baht a dollar buys, and the last link in every chain on this board: it is the exchange rate that turns a US portfolio into money you can actually spend. A stronger dollar hurts your stocks and helps this, which is why 'my stocks fell' and 'I got poorer' are different sentences.

nodes.label: WTI crude
nodes.up: Energy costs more — inflation nobody can argue away, and a tax on importers
nodes.what: The US oil benchmark. Oil is the input to almost everything physical, so it feeds inflation directly rather than through expectations. It is also the one macro variable that moves on geopolitics in an afternoon.

nodes.label: Gold
nodes.up: Gold is bid — real rates fell, or trust in something official did
nodes.what: The asset with no cash flow, no counterparty and no government. It tracks two things: the real yield it competes against, and how much people trust the institutions that issue the alternatives. Central banks have been the marginal buyer for years.

nodes.label: Silver
nodes.up: Silver is bid — gold's story plus industrial demand, at twice the volatility
nodes.what: Half precious metal, half industrial input — roughly 55% of demand is electronics, solar and brazing. It follows gold but overshoots in both directions, and it carries an economic-growth signal gold does not.

nodes.label: Copper
nodes.up: Copper is bid — somebody somewhere is actually building things
nodes.what: The metal in every wire, motor and transformer, which is why it is called the one commodity with a degree in economics. It is mostly a read on Chinese construction, and increasingly on electrical grid buildout for data centres.

nodes.label: S&P 500
nodes.up: US large caps are up — the world's default risk asset is being bought
nodes.what: The 500 largest US listed companies, and the benchmark almost all global money is measured against. About 70% of the world's investable equity value sits in the US, so this is not one market among many.

nodes.label: Nasdaq 100
nodes.up: Long-duration growth is bid — the part of the market rates hurt most
nodes.what: The hundred largest non-financial Nasdaq companies — technology, in practice. Their profits are further in the future than the market's, which makes this the most rate-sensitive large index there is.

nodes.label: Semiconductors
nodes.up: Chips are bid — the cycle that leads every other cycle is expanding
nodes.what: The semiconductor complex, which turns before the rest of manufacturing does and is now the physical bottleneck of the AI build-out. It is also the single largest geopolitical concentration risk on this board.

nodes.label: Nikkei 225
nodes.up: Japanese equities are up — usually because the yen went down
nodes.what: Japan's headline index, dominated by exporters. It has an unusually tight and mechanical relationship with the yen: a weaker yen inflates their foreign earnings when translated home, so the index and the currency trade almost as one instrument.

nodes.label: Shanghai Composite
nodes.up: Chinese equities are up — domestic policy support is landing, or being believed
nodes.what: Mainland China's main index, driven far more by Beijing's policy stance and by domestic retail flows than by global risk appetite. It is the one large market that regularly moves opposite to everything else.

nodes.label: Emerging markets
nodes.up: EM equities are up — the dollar let go, or growth turned up
nodes.what: Equities across the developing world in one instrument. It is best understood as a leveraged bet against the dollar: EM borrows in dollars and earns in local currency, so the dollar's direction usually matters more than local earnings do.

nodes.label: Thai equities
nodes.up: Thai equities are up — foreign money came back, or oil fell
nodes.what: The Stock Exchange of Thailand. Thailand imports its energy and exports tourism and goods, so it is hurt by expensive oil and helped by a weak dollar — and it moves on foreign flows far more than on anything domestic.

nodes.label: Bitcoin
nodes.up: Bitcoin is bid — the purest read on how much spare money exists
nodes.what: The highest-beta liquidity asset there is: no cash flow, no earnings, no floor except what somebody will pay. That makes it the cleanest instrument on this board for reading global liquidity.

nodes.label: 30-year mortgage
nodes.up: Housing got more expensive to finance — the bond market reaching a household
nodes.what: The average US 30-year fixed mortgage rate. This is the step where a bond yield stops being a financial abstraction: it is priced off the 10-year, and it decides whether a family can afford to move.

nodes.label: Corporate borrowing cost
nodes.up: Companies pay more to refinance — buybacks and capex get cut before jobs do
nodes.what: What an ordinary investment-grade company actually pays to borrow: the government yield plus its credit spread. It is the number that decides whether a board approves a factory, a buyback, or neither.

nodes.label: Brent crude
nodes.up: The global oil benchmark is up — the one the rest of the world actually pays
nodes.what: The seaborne oil benchmark, and the price most of the world imports at. Its gap to WTI is a read on US export capacity.

nodes.label: US natural gas
nodes.up: Gas is up — heating, power and fertiliser all get dearer
nodes.what: Henry Hub gas, which sets US electricity and fertiliser costs and is now tied to data-centre power demand.

nodes.label: Russell 2000
nodes.up: US small caps are up — domestic, indebted and floating-rate, so this reads credit
nodes.what: US small companies. They borrow at floating rates and sell domestically, so they respond to credit conditions far more directly than large caps.

nodes.label: Euro Stoxx 50
nodes.up: European large caps are up
nodes.what: The euro area's blue chips — banks, industrials and luxury, and heavily exposed to both Chinese demand and energy costs.

nodes.label: Hang Seng
nodes.up: Hong Kong is up — the foreign-money read on China
nodes.what: Where global investors express a China view, since the mainland market is mostly domestic. It often moves before Shanghai does.

nodes.label: KOSPI
nodes.up: Korea is up — the world's export order book is filling
nodes.what: Korea's index, dominated by memory chips and shipbuilding. Its export data is released early each month and is one of the cleanest real-time reads on world trade there is.

nodes.label: TAIEX
nodes.up: Taiwan is up — the AI supply chain is being paid
nodes.what: Taiwan's index, which is substantially one company's supply chain. The most concentrated single point of failure in the world economy.

nodes.label: Nifty 50
nodes.up: India is up — the domestic-demand alternative to China
nodes.what: India's benchmark. Driven by domestic savings flows rather than foreign money, which makes it unusually insulated from the dollar.

nodes.label: Ethereum
nodes.up: Ether is bid — bitcoin's move plus the risk appetite inside crypto
nodes.what: The second crypto asset, and a higher-beta version of the first: it carries bitcoin's liquidity signal plus speculative appetite within crypto itself.

nodes.label: EUR / USD
nodes.up: The euro is stronger against the dollar
nodes.what: The most traded currency pair, and about 58% of the dollar index by weight — so DXY is largely this, inverted.

nodes.label: Germany 10-year
nodes.up: The euro area's risk-free rate is rising
nodes.what: The Bund — the euro area's benchmark safe asset, and the anchor every other European government bond is priced against.

nodes.label: 3-month T-bill
nodes.up: Short money is dearer — the market has moved its Fed expectations up
nodes.what: What the government pays to borrow for three months. Traded rather than set, so it moves ahead of the Fed when the market changes its mind.
